mods.name: Data Center
mods.tagline: Server racks, rack servers, cable trays and the room around them.
mods.summary: 19-inch racks in 24U and 42U, ten rack servers (six are working automation blocks), 38 overhead cable-tray blocks and 19 room pieces: raised floor, an in-row cooler, aisle doors and roof panels, power and signs.

children.text: . Its C# scripts add three things: the sequenced KVM motion, a KVM that waits for the rack doors, and the Programmable server's script editor. Space Engineers 2 runs mod scripts only when the game is started with
Library → Space Engineers 2 → Properties → Launch Options, add
with and without scripts, so you can switch at any time.
every player and the server should use the same setting. The differences are visual only.

features.title: Server racks
features.body: Two heights: 24U with 4 server slots, and 42U with 8 slots, a fan tray and an overhead cable-tray mount. Each comes as an open frame, with split front doors, or with front and rear doors. The perforated doors swing 85° toward the aisle.

video.caption: The split front doors swing open to 85 degrees and close again, timed like the game's door blocks.

features.title: Working rack servers
features.body: The Timer, Event Controller, Status Display (an LCD), UPS (a battery with two swappable Power Cell bays) and Programmable servers work like the vanilla blocks. The KVM console is the sixth working server. Compute, Storage, Network Switch and Blanking Panel are there to fill the rack.

image.alt: Ten server blocks lined up in two rows on a gray floor.
image.caption: All ten server blocks side by side. The front row is the hardware (compute, storage, switch, blank panel, UPS); the back row holds the working blocks: timer, event controller, status display, programmable and KVM.

features.title: Cable trays
features.body: Overhead wire-basket trays in four cable densities. The set has straights, turns, tees, crosses, reducers, and drops that run cables down into the racks. Cable lanes match at every joint. The data cables take the block paint.

image.alt: Wire-basket cable trays hanging from rods above a row of racks, with cables dropping into the racks.
image.caption: Cable trays hung from ceiling rods over a row of racks: a tee branching off, reducers stepping the bundle down, and drops that run cables down into each rack.

features.title: Room pieces
features.body: Raised floor tiles, an in-row cooler whose fans spin up when powered, a PDU cabinet, rack power strips, sliding containment doors, roof panels, and aisle signs and rack labels with editable text. With them you can build a contained cold aisle like the ones in real data centers.

video.caption: The aisle's sliding door opening and closing, seen from inside the contained cold aisle.

features.title: KVM console
features.body: Switch the KVM server on and its keyboard drawer slides out and the screen folds up. With scripts on, the drawer slides first and then the screen lifts with a small spring. It waits for the rack doors to open, and if you switch it mid-motion it reverses from where it is.

video.caption: The KVM drawer slides out, the screen lifts and settles with a small spring, then it folds away and the drawer slides back in. This is the scripted motion.

features.title: Damage models
features.body: Every block has fracture zones, a dented model for when it is damaged and a broken one for when it is destroyed. They follow the vanilla fracture rules.

image.alt: An intact compute server next to a dented, damaged one.
image.caption: An intact compute server beside a damaged one. Every block has its own dented model, which the game swaps in when the block takes damage, and a broken model for when it is destroyed.

children.text: Build a hall in this order
Racks, the cooler, the PDU cabinet and the doors all stand on the tiles. Put perforated tiles where the cold air comes up.
Racks, the in-row cooler and the PDU cabinet share one footprint (1.0 m wide, 1.25 m deep, 2.5 m tall), so a row stays on a 1.0 m pitch.
1.0, 1.5 or 2.0 m. Doors and roof panels come in each width.
with the sliding containment doors at the row ends and roof panels along the top.
on hanger rods 0.5 m above the rack tops and drop cables into each rack.
Aisle signs and rack labels are LCDs: type your own text, and paint the frame blue (cold) or red (hot).
Data Center is being tested in game. Block names, costs and PCU may change before the first release, so don’t build anything you can’t rebuild.

blogPosts.title: How the Data Center was made
blogPosts.subtitle: The saved renders, from the first mockup to the finished hall.
blogPosts.excerpt: The saved renders from the Data Center build, in order: racks, servers, cable trays, room shell, room equipment and the finished hall, with a note on what changed at each step.

cover.alt: Whole hall / hero shots: Plan 3 Task 12: doors outside

children.text: Data Center went from a first mockup to a finished hall in about three days. The generators saved a render at most steps. This post goes through them by family.

The first images were quick mockups to settle proportions: how wide a 42U rack is next to a vanilla block, how deep a server is, how a door leaf hangs. They were never meant to ship. The second round switched them to the game's material roles so they matched vanilla blocks.

body.caption: The 42U rack, first mockup against the final block.

after.alt: Server rack 42U (and doors): Room merge: rails and PDU strips

children.text: The rack had to be 1.0 m wide

The first rack export came out 4 cells (1.0 m) wide so a 2-cell server could be centered with mountable sides. That set the pitch for the rest of the hall: racks, the in-row cooler and the PDU cabinet all share the same 1.0 m by 1.25 m footprint, so rows stay on a 1.0 m grid.

Six of the ten servers are working automation blocks (timer, event controller, status display, UPS, programmable and KVM). The other four are there to fill the rack. Each server got layered bezels, LEDs and rear panels, because a rack of flat boxes looked cheap.
The cable trays have their own post. The room came last: raised floor, containment doors, the cooler, PDUs and signs, then the two-aisle hall used for the screenshots.

blogPosts.title: Making a KVM drawer feel right
blogPosts.subtitle: Moving the drawer and the screen one after the other.
blogPosts.excerpt: Without scripts, the KVM drawer slides and the screen folds at the same time, and it looks wrong. With scripts, the drawer slides first, pauses, and then the screen lifts with a small spring.

cover.alt: A rack-mounted keyboard drawer pulled out with its screen folded up.
cover.caption: The KVM drawer pulled out with its screen folded up. With scripts on, the drawer slides out first and then the screen lifts.

children.text: A rack-mounted KVM is a keyboard and a fold-down monitor on a sliding drawer. In a real rack you pull the drawer out until it stops, then lift the screen. Two motions, one after the other.
The game's animation data can only move parts at the same time. Without scripts, the drawer slides and the screen folds together. It works, but it doesn't look like the real thing.

video.caption: The KVM drawer slides out, the screen lifts and settles with a small spring, then it folds away and the drawer slides back in. This is the scripted motion.

children.text: With scripts on, a small sequencer runs the motion:
A short pause, like a real drawer stopping at the end of its rails.
The screen folds up and settles with a small spring at the top.
Switching it off runs the same steps backwards: fold first, then slide in. Switch it halfway through and it reverses from where it is instead of snapping.

A KVM behind closed rack doors would push straight through them, so the script waits. The KVM stays stowed while the doors are closed, comes out shortly after they are fully open, and stows quickly as soon as they start to close. Only a door on the KVM's side counts.
Everything here needs the game to be started with
. Without it, the KVM uses the plain data-only motion, and nothing breaks. Saves are identical either way.

blogPosts.title: Cable trays that always line up
blogPosts.subtitle: 38 blocks in four cable densities, with lanes that match at every joint.
blogPosts.excerpt: How the 38 cable-tray blocks keep each cable bundle in the same lane across joints, and what reducers and drops do.

cover.alt: Wire-basket cable trays hanging from rods above a row of racks, with cables dropping into the racks.
cover.caption: Cable trays hung from ceiling rods over a row of racks: a tee branching off, reducers stepping the bundle down, and drops that run cables down into each rack.

children.text: Cable trays look wrong when the cables don't line up: a bundle jumps lanes at a joint, or ends in mid-air. So we designed the trays around fixed lanes first and shapes second.
Each tray comes in four densities:
(adds yellow fiber and gray power) and
(adds a second data layer and black power). Every density puts its bundles in the same lanes, so a Low straight joined to a Low turn always matches.
steps the density down one level, and reducers chain. You can also join two densities directly: the shared lanes match and the extra lanes end cleanly at the joint.
carries two waterfalls of cable down into a full rack's front cable managers. Over a 24U half rack, a Long Drop Chute under the Drop makes up the height.

image.caption: Cable trays hung from ceiling rods over a row of racks: a tee branching off, reducers stepping the bundle down, and drops that run cables down into each rack.

children.text: Hanger rods snap only onto the tray’s rod plates. Hang a run 0.5 m above the rack tops, centered 0.125 m in front of the rack center, and the drops land in the cable managers.

aboutPage.title: About Rioku Labs
aboutPage.intro: Rioku Labs is a small team making mods for Space Engineers 2. We build the blocks we want to play with, test them in the game, and share the source.

children.text: If something looks like it opens, it opens. Doors, drawers, fans and screens do their job in the game, not only in a render.
Blocks should sit next to the game's own without standing out: same scale, same build stages, and damage that breaks them apart properly.
We model and texture everything ourselves. Scripts are always optional, so a mod still works on servers that turn them off.
Our mods are GPL-3.0. The source goes public when a mod is released.
, and nothing ships until it has been built, broken and rebuilt in a test world.
